Alpha Particle. This is a helium-four nucleus consisting of two protons and two neutrons bound together. An alpha particle is ejected from certain radioactive atoms during decay and is one of the three main types of radioactive emission, alongside beta and gamma radiation. Alpha particles are relatively massive and carry a strong positive charge, making them the least penetrating but most ionizing form of radiation.

An alpha particle is identical to a helium-four nucleus without its electrons. It is produced during alpha decay when heavy unstable nuclei shed mass and energy by expelling an alpha particle. The term was named by Rutherford, who used alpha particles as projectiles in his famous gold foil experiment, revealing the nuclear model of the atom.

Cannot penetrate paper or skin due to its large mass and strong positive charge. Yet alpha particles are extremely dangerous if ingested or inhaled. They ionize surrounding matter intensely due to their high charge, creating a trail of excited and ionized atoms along their path. Uranium, thorium, and radon commonly undergo alpha decay, making alpha radiation prevalent in natural radioactivity.

Alpha particles are stopped by a few centimeters of air or a sheet of paper, allowing their range to be measured and studied easily. Rutherford's gold foil experiment used alpha particles scattered by gold atoms to reveal the concentration of mass in a tiny nucleus, overturning the plum pudding model of the atom. The term alpha originates from the Greek letter naming scheme for three types of radiation discovered in the early nineteen hundreds. Understanding alpha particles was central to revealing the existence of the atomic nucleus.
